Theories in the behavioural sciences often define their constructs too loosely
to measure, state claims that no result could contradict and survive a failed
test by adding an assumption that protects them. `theoryforge` holds a theory
as a structured file of constructs, propositions, predictions, rival accounts
and test outcomes, and computes what that file commits the theory to. It checks
how completely the file states what a checklist of criteria drawn from the
methodology literature asks for, derives the independencies and signed effects
its causal graph implies, grades how risky each prediction is and how severely
it has been tested, and appraises, by fixed rules that borrow Lakatos's terms,
whether an amendment adds content or only shields the theory from an anomaly.

```{r setup}
library(theoryforge)
```

## A worked result

The package includes a deliberately underspecified theory of motivation.
`tf_example_path()` gives the path of each example, and `tf_example_names()`
lists them. Running the checklist on the theory gives its checklist score, the
range of scores that equal weights or one weight halved or doubled would give,
its gate and the items it does not pass.

```{r worked-result}
weak <- tf_read(tf_example_path("weak-theory.theory.yaml"))
report <- tf_check(weak)

report$aggregate_score
report$aggregate_range
report$gate

open_items <- Filter(function(item) item$status != "pass", report$items)
data.frame(
  item = vapply(open_items, function(item) item$id, character(1)),
  status = vapply(open_items, function(item) item$status, character(1)),
  if_failed = vapply(open_items, function(item) item$severity_if_fail, character(1))
)
```

The gate is blocked because two items that the checklist treats as blockers
failed. The theory's one prediction, 'Motivated people exist', is typed as an
existence claim, and the falsifiability item reads that label: no prediction is
typed point, interval or directional. The prediction also cites no proposition
from which it would follow. To unblock the gate, the author would state a
prediction that rules out some result, such as a direction or a bounded range of
an effect, type it accordingly and derive it from a proposition. The warnings name the
remaining work. Motivation and Drive are defined in nearly the same words and
would have to be merged or defined apart. Neither construct has a measure or a
stated scope, and the one proposition is an association without a mechanism.
The `development_roadmap` view of `tf_diagram()` draws the same list as an
ordered worklist.

The checklist score describes how completely the file states what checklist
`r report$checklist_version` asks for. Most items read whether a field is filled
in or how a prediction is labelled, and stated claims are checked against the
causal graph. Test outcomes are read only by the parsimony item, the weights are
conventions, and no study has established what difference between two scores is
meaningful. The score does not show that the theory is true or well reasoned.

The checklist score is a mean of the item scores under conventional weights. The
gate reports whether either blocking item failed: at least one prediction is
typed point, interval or directional, and every prediction cites declared
propositions whose graph entails any claim it states, with no stated phenomenon
contradicted. The labels are the author's and are not checked against the
statements. A passing gate does not show that the theory is true or well
reasoned. A claim that the graph leaves unread because it has a feedback loop is
not checked, and the derivation chain then warns without blocking the gate.

## Reading and validating a theory

The rest of this vignette reads a theory of modality switching in grounded
conceptual processing. Five constructs are linked by four causal propositions.
Sensorimotor experience with a concept drives the activation of a
modality-specific perceptual system, and that activation both raises the cost of
switching modality between consecutive trials and eases conceptual access, which
familiarity with the word form eases as well.

```{r read}
theory <- tf_read(tf_example_path("modality-switching.theory.yaml"))
```

`tf_validate()` returns `TRUE` invisibly when the theory is valid and otherwise
stops with a message that lists every problem. With the default `full = FALSE`,
it checks the structure: the required fields, the allowed values of each
enumerated field, that every top-level field is one the schema defines and that
each collection is a list. `full = TRUE` adds the referential checks, that ids
are unique and that every reference between constructs, propositions,
predictions, alternatives, assumptions, evidence and test outcomes names a
declared id, and then checks the type of every other field, the form of each
claim and whether the bounds of each prediction fit its type. The calls below
wrap it in `isTRUE()` to show the result.

```{r validate}
isTRUE(tf_validate(theory))
isTRUE(tf_validate(theory, full = TRUE))
```

A prediction that cites a proposition the theory never declares passes the
structural check, since every required field is present, and only the full pass
reports it. The message counts entries from 0, so `prediction[0]` is the first
prediction.

```{r validate-failure, error = TRUE}
broken <- theory
broken$predictions[[1]]$derives_from <- list("p_missing")
isTRUE(tf_validate(broken))
tf_validate(broken, full = TRUE)
```

## Identifying a theory by its content

`tf_content_hash()` returns the SHA-256 digest of the theory's content written
in a canonical form. Two files that hold the same theory have the same hash,
whatever their layout, comments, key order or format, and any change to a value
changes it. The preregistration and the dossier both print it, so a reader
can check that the theory file in hand is the one a document describes. The
Python package's `content_hash()` gives the same digest.

```{r hash}
tf_content_hash(theory)
```

A theory can record its own hash under `version$content_hash`, which the hash
leaves out of the content it digests. The full validation then compares the
recorded hash with the content, so an edit made after the hash was recorded is
reported.

```{r hash-recorded, error = TRUE}
recorded <- theory
recorded$version$content_hash <- tf_content_hash(recorded)
isTRUE(tf_validate(recorded, full = TRUE))

recorded$constructs[[1]]$definition <- paste(
  recorded$constructs[[1]]$definition, "Edited after registration."
)
tf_validate(recorded, full = TRUE)
```

## The checklist

`tf_check()` scores the theory against the checklist the package ships, version
`r tf_check(theory)$checklist_version`, whose twelve items each test one
criterion drawn from the methodology literature. Each item has the status
`"pass"`, `"warn"`, `"fail"` or `"n/a"`, the last for an item with nothing to
assess, such as the parsimony of a theory that adds no assumption to answer an
anomaly. An `"n/a"` item has a `NULL` score.

```{r check}
report <- tf_check(theory)

report$checklist_version
report$aggregate_score
report$aggregate_range
report$coverage
report$gate

data.frame(
  item = vapply(report$items, function(item) item$id, character(1)),
  status = vapply(report$items, function(item) item$status, character(1)),
  score = vapply(report$items, function(item) {
    if (is.null(item$score)) NA_real_ else item$score
  }, numeric(1))
)
```

The checklist score, `aggregate_score`, is the weighted mean of the applicable
items' scores, on a scale of 0 to 100, and the coverage is the share of the
checklist's weight that applied. The weights are a convention, so
`aggregate_range` gives the lowest and the highest score over the checklist's
weights, equal weights and each applicable item's weight halved and then
doubled with the others unchanged. The range is the extremes of these weightings
and not an interval for the score, and the choices made in coding the file and
the constants of the claim-form rubric lie outside it. A score whose range is
wide depends on the convention more than one whose range is narrow. The score is
compensatory, since a high score on one item offsets a low score on another. The
gate is not. It is `"blocked"` when an item marked as a blocker fails, `"pass"`
otherwise, and `"advisory"` for a theory whose maturity is `draft`. The
derivation chain warns, without blocking the gate, when a feedback loop leaves a
prediction's or a phenomenon's claim unread, as `tf_check()` does by default,
and `tf_check(theory, cycles = "sigma")` reads such claims by sigma-separation.
The article
[Methodological foundations](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/r/articles/methodology.html)
sets out each item, its supporting literature and how its score is computed.

`tf_report()` returns the same result as a string, in JSON by default or as an
HTML fragment for a web page with `format = "html"`.

## Building a theory

A theory's `maturity` field records its stage as `building`, `developing` or
`testing`, or as `draft`, which makes the checklist's gate advisory.
`tf_theory()` starts an empty theory, and the builders `tf_add_construct()`,
`tf_add_proposition()`, `tf_add_prediction()`, `tf_add_phenomenon()`,
`tf_add_alternative()`, `tf_add_assumption()`, `tf_add_evidence()`,
`tf_add_test_outcome()` and `tf_set_formal_model()` add to it. Each returns a
modified copy and records a step in the theory's provenance log, so the steps
compose with the native pipe and the original object stays as it was.

```{r build}
built <- tf_theory("panic-demo", "A demonstration theory of panic") |>
  tf_add_construct("c_arousal", "Physiological arousal",
                   "Bodily activation in response to a stressor.",
                   measurement = "heart rate variability",
                   boundary_conditions = "awake adults") |>
  tf_add_construct("c_threat", "Perceived threat",
                   "Appraised danger of bodily sensations.",
                   measurement = "self-report appraisal scale",
                   boundary_conditions = "awake adults") |>
  tf_add_proposition("p1", "c_arousal", "c_threat", "increases",
                     mechanism = "Activation raises the salience of threat cues.") |>
  tf_add_prediction("h1", "Arousal raises threat appraisal.", "directional",
                    derives_from = "p1",
                    claim = list(kind = "effect", x = "c_arousal",
                                 y = "c_threat", sign = "positive"))

isTRUE(tf_validate(built, full = TRUE))
do.call(rbind, lapply(built$provenance, as.data.frame))
```

The type of a prediction names the form of its claim. An `existence` prediction
asserts that an effect or relation exists, without a direction, and a
`directional` one asserts a sign or an order. An `interval` prediction asserts
that a quantity lies in a stated range, and a `point` prediction asserts one
value, with the tolerance that measurement requires. `bounds` states the region,
and the full validation checks that it fits the type, so an existence prediction
takes none. A `claim` states the prediction in a form the causal reading can
check against the propositions, as the article
[Developing and testing a theory](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/r/articles/developing-and-testing.html)
shows.

How a theory is encoded decides what the package derives from it. A `moderates`
proposition states that its `from` modifies the effect of other causes on its
`to`, and the causal graph reads it as an edge without a sign from the
moderator to the outcome. The relation it modifies keeps its sign, but every
effect of the moderator on that outcome is left open, including a main effect
the theory also states, even when that main effect is encoded as a signed
proposition of its own, since an edge has a sign only when every proposition
that states it gives it one. A theory whose main effect matters can record the
interaction in the `functional_form` of the proposition it modifies, or in a
prediction's statement, at the cost of a graph that does not show it. Whether a
relation that a proposition states is also entered as a prediction is the
encoder's choice too, and it changes the hypotheses that the preregistration
lists.

`tf_add_alternative()` registers a rival account, which can state propositions
of its own over the theory's constructs. A prediction that names the rival in
`diagnostic_vs` declares that it discriminates between the two, and the
checklist checks that declaration against the rival's propositions.

```{r build-rival}
built <- built |>
  tf_add_alternative(
    "alt_reverse", "Threat drives arousal",
    propositions = list(list(id = "r1", from = "c_threat", to = "c_arousal",
                             relation = "increases"))
  )
length(built$alternatives[[1]]$propositions)
```

`tf_write()` saves a theory as JSON when the path ends in `.json` and as YAML
otherwise. The file reads back as the same theory, with the same content hash,
in R and in Python.

```{r io}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
tf_write(built, path)
identical(tf_content_hash(tf_read(path)), tf_content_hash(built))
```

## Starting from a DAGitty diagram

Many causal theories are first drawn as a diagram in
[DAGitty](https://dagitty.net)
([Textor et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw341)).
`tf_read_dagitty()` reads its model code and returns a theory with one construct
for each variable and one proposition for each edge. An arrow becomes `causes`,
or `increases` or `decreases` when `relation` says so, and `<->` becomes
`associates`. The theory has the maturity `draft`, and it is not valid until
every construct has a definition, which a diagram cannot supply.

FAIR theory specifies a theory as a findable, accessible, interoperable and
reusable digital object in a public archive
([Van Lissa et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1177/17456916251401850)). Its
worked example of self-determination theory, in the theorytools package
([Van Lissa, 2025](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.theorytools)), keeps
the diagram in a DAGitty file and the construct definitions in a CSV table
beside it. The example below imports the modality-switching graph in that
form. The two files
are written out as text so that the code runs as shown, and in practice each
would be read from its file.

```{r dagitty}
dagitty_file <- "dag {
  sensorimotor_experience -> modality_activation
  modality_activation -> switch_cost
  modality_activation -> conceptual_access
  lexical_familiarity -> conceptual_access
}"
definitions <- read.csv(text = "Concept,Synonym,Definition,Operationalization
Sensorimotor experience,,Perceptual and motor engagement with the referent of a concept.,Perceptual strength ratings
Modality activation,,Recruitment of one modality's perceptual system while a word is understood.,Interference from a concurrent load
Switch cost,,The extra time taken when consecutive trials address different modalities.,Switch-minus-repeat response time
Conceptual access,,The speed with which the meaning of a word becomes available.,Semantic categorisation latency",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

imported <- tf_read_dagitty(
  dagitty_file,
  id = "modality-switching-fair",
  title = "Modality switching in grounded conceptual processing",
  relation = "increases"
)
key <- gsub(" ", "_", tolower(trimws(definitions$Concept)))
for (i in seq_along(imported$constructs)) {
  row <- match(imported$constructs[[i]]$id, key)
  if (!is.na(row)) {
    imported$constructs[[i]]$label <- trimws(definitions$Concept[row])
    imported$constructs[[i]]$definition <- trimws(definitions$Definition[row])
  }
}

ids <- vapply(imported$constructs, function(c) c$id, character(1))
defined <- vapply(imported$constructs, function(c) nzchar(c$definition), logical(1))
ids[!defined]
```

The table names its concepts in words, and the diagram in identifiers, so each
concept is matched to a construct by its name lower-cased with spaces replaced
by underscores. One construct, lexical familiarity, has no row in the table and
is listed above. The operationalisation column is left out, because it describes
measures in prose, whereas a construct's `measurement` lists indicator names
that the lavaan syntax uses as columns of the data. The merge edits the theory's
fields directly, so the provenance log records the import and not the
definitions.

With the missing definition added, the theory validates in full. Its gate is
advisory, since its maturity is `draft`, and the checklist reports what the
diagram could not supply: a prediction that forbids some result, measures, scope
conditions and mechanisms.

```{r dagitty-check}
imported$constructs[[match("lexical_familiarity", ids)]]$definition <-
  "How well established the form of a word is for a reader."
isTRUE(tf_validate(imported, full = TRUE))

imported_report <- tf_check(imported)
imported_report$gate
Filter(function(item) item$status != "pass", imported_report$items) |>
  vapply(function(item) paste(item$id, item$status), character(1))
```

The graph alone already commits the imported theory to the conditional
independencies and the untestable causal directions that the article
[Developing and testing a theory](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/r/articles/developing-and-testing.html)
derives for the full modality-switching theory, since the two share a graph. The
`causal_dag` view of `tf_diagram()` writes a theory back in DAGitty's syntax,
keeping its directed edges, its associations and any variable marked as latent.

## Screening constructs for redundancy

`tf_redundancy_check()` compares the definitions of every pair of constructs by
the words they share, through the Jaccard similarity and the overlap
coefficient, and returns the pairs sorted by descending similarity. A pair is
flagged `"review"` when its definitions are near duplicates or one is contained
in the other, which suggests that two names cover one construct. It also flags
two constructs that carry one label, and a pair in which every measure listed
for one construct is also listed for the other, since data from those measures
cannot tell the two apart. The `reason` column names the grounds of each flag.
The comparison of definitions is lexical, so a definition reworded into other
words passes it.

```{r redundancy}
head(tf_redundancy_check(theory), 3)
```

`tf_embedding_redundancy()` compares the definitions by the cosine similarity of
vectors from an embedder that the caller supplies, such as a language model.
Here, a toy bag-of-words embedder stands in for one.

```{r embedding-redundancy}
vocab <- c("bodily", "activation", "appraised", "danger", "salience")
embedder <- function(definition) {
  words <- strsplit(tolower(definition), "[^a-z]+")[[1]]
  vapply(vocab, function(w) sum(words == w), numeric(1))
}
tf_embedding_redundancy(built, embedder)
```

## Drawing the theory

`tf_diagram()` returns one of ten views of the theory. The graph views are
Graphviz DOT, which any Graphviz tool renders. The nomological network draws
each proposition as an edge labelled with its id and relation.

```{r diagram}
cat(tf_diagram(theory, type = "nomological_net"))
```

`tf_render_diagram()` returns the DOT as a DiagrammeR widget for the viewer and
for R Markdown, or as an SVG string with `as = "svg"`. The packages it uses are
optional and listed in Suggests. The figure below is drawn from the DOT above.

```{r diagram-render, results = "asis", eval = has_diagram}
cat(
  '<div class="tf-figure tf-diagram">',
  tf_render_diagram(theory, "nomological_net", as = "svg"),
  '</div>',
  sep = ""
)
```

The `causal_dag` view writes the directed relations and the associations in
DAGitty's syntax, for [dagitty.net](https://dagitty.net) and the dagitty
package, and `tf_render_diagram()` does not draw it.

```{r causal-dag}
cat(tf_diagram(theory, type = "causal_dag"))
```

## Next steps

The article
[Developing and testing a theory](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/r/articles/developing-and-testing.html)
appraises an amendment and derives what a theory's causal graph commits it to,
from its implied independencies to the results that would tell it from a rival,
and then preregisters it, grades its tests and assembles the dossier.
[Mapping the literature](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/r/articles/literature.html)
maps a corpus of publications against a theory, and
[Browser apps](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/r/articles/app.html)
describes the two apps that run the packages without an installation.

## Two languages, one specification

A Python package of the same name implements the same
[specification](https://github.com/pablobernabeu/theoryforge/blob/main/API_SPEC.md),
with the same function names without the `tf_` prefix, apart from `new_theory()`
for `tf_theory()`. The deterministic
functions, from validation and the checklist to the causal reading, the
preregistration and the dossier, are checked against shared expected outputs, so
the two languages give the same results. The helpers that depend on a network
service, an embedder or a renderer (`tf_fetch_corpus()`, `tf_osf_push()`,
`tf_embedding_redundancy()` and `tf_render_diagram()`) can differ between them.
